raw_case_text:
A 53-year-old morbidly obese female with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department (ED), with a sudden onset of loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, and altered sensorium for two days, which was associated with high-grade fever and vomiting. At admission, she was unconscious (Glasgow coma scale, or GCS, score = 5); had tachypnea (respiratory rate, or RR, 30-35 minute-1), tachycardia (heart rate, or HR, 114 bpm), and blood pressure (BP) 153/90 mmHg; was maintaining oxygen saturation of 94% to 94% (on room air) on spontaneous respiration; and was passing urine output around 40-50 mL/hour. Given airway protection, tracheal intubation was performed immediately. Post intubation, the GCS was 6. Noncontrast computerized tomography (NCCT) of the brain revealed right basal ganglia bleeding with intraventricular hemorrhage (Figure 1).
Then she was transferred to ICU, where cerebral protection strategy (head-up position, neck in a neutral position, osmotic diuretics, mean arterial pressure (MAP) 85-90 mm Hg, normoxia, normocarbia, euglycemia, normothermia, and maintenance of sodium (Na+) levels between 145 and 155 mEq/L) and further supportive care was initiated. Laboratory evaluation at admission is summarized in Table 1. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray (CXR) was normal.   
After a few days of ICU admission, she started spiking high-grade temperature (core temperature as high as 106-107  F), which was associated with rhabdomyolysis (serum creatine kinase (CK-total) = 10,000 IU/L), stage III acute kidney injury (AKI, requiring five sessions of renal replacement therapy), and coagulopathy (requiring blood component therapy). On workup, cultures turned out to be sterile. Other possibilities of hyperthermia (such as drug toxicity) were ruled out. NCCT head was repeated, which did not reveal any hematoma expansion. Workup for COVID-19 was also negative. On account of a history of fever with chill and myalgia around a week before ED admission, a tropical workup was sent for malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus, in which serology (IgM antibodies) for dengue turned out to be positive. Gradually, the temperature trends, renal functions, and coagulopathy recovered. In intercurrent issues, she had septic shock (secondary to ventilator-associated pneumonia and grade IV pressure injury in the sacral region) and neuromuscular weakness, resulting in prolonged weaning. Eventually, the patient was discharged after six months of ICU stay in tracheostomized condition, with a GCS score of 9, accepting Ryle's tube feeding and passing adequate urine output.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old morbidly obese female with hypertension presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of sudden loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, altered sensorium, high-grade fever, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Approximately 1 week prior to emergency department presentation, the patient experienced a febrile illness with chills and myalgia. Two days prior to admission, she developed sudden-onset loss of consciousness, left-sided hemiparesis, and altered sensorium accompanied by high-grade fever and vomiting. A few days after ICU admission, she developed extreme hyperthermia (core temperatures reaching 106-107 °F).
subjective.past_medical_history: History of morbid obesity and systemic hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for prodromal fever, chills, and myalgia (1 week prior), followed by sudden loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, vomiting, and extreme high-grade fever.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient was unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 5 (improving to 6 post-intubation), tachypnea (respiratory rate 30-35/min), tachycardia (heart rate 114 bpm), hypertension (blood pressure 153/90 mmHg), SpO2 94% on room air, left-sided hemiparesis, and urine output of 40-50 mL/hour. In the ICU, her core temperature spiked to 106-107 °F.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission ECG showed sinus tachycardia and chest X-ray was normal. During extreme ICU hyperthermia, laboratory workup revealed severe rhabdomyolysis (total serum creatine kinase 10,000 IU/L), Stage III acute kidney injury, and coagulopathy. Cultures were sterile and COVID-19 testing was negative. Tropical fever panel (testing for malaria, typhoid fever, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus) was positive for dengue IgM antibodies and negative for typhoid and other tropical pathogens.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission non-contrast head CT demonstrated a right basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage with intraventricular hemorrhage extension; repeat non-contrast head CT during extreme hyperthermia showed no hematoma expansion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute dengue fever (confirmed by positive dengue IgM serology) complicated by spontaneous right basal ganglia intracerebral and intraventricular hemorrhage (confirmed on head NCCT), extreme central/infectious hyperthermia (106-107 °F), rhabdomyolysis (CK 10,000 IU/L), Stage III acute kidney injury, and coagulopathy. Typhoid fever, malaria, leptospirosis, chikungunya, scrub typhus, COVID-19, bacterial sepsis, and drug toxicity were ruled out. Management included emergency endotracheal intubation, neuroprotective ICU care (head-of-bed elevation, osmotic diuretics, MAP 85-90 mmHg, hyperosmolar sodium target 145-155 mEq/L), blood component transfusions for coagulopathy, and 5 sessions of renal replacement therapy. Her fever, renal function, and coagulopathy recovered, and after a prolonged 6-month ICU stay complicated by ventilator-associated pneumonia, sacral grade IV pressure injury, and critical illness neuromuscular weakness, she was discharged with a tracheostomy, GCS 9, nasogastric tube feeding, and normal urine output.
